sections.heading: Wearing schedules, adaptation, and compliance
sections.body:
**Wear schedule** is how long a lens stays on the eye; **replacement schedule** is how long before it is thrown away.

- **Daily wear**: removed before sleep
- **Extended wear**: overnight, typically up to 6 nights; after each scheduled removal the eyes rest lens-free for at least one night
- **Continuous wear**: silicone hydrogel lenses up to 30 nights
- Sleeping in daily-wear lenses raises the risk of infection, ulcers, and neovascularization

**Adaptation**: soft lenses take several days; RGP lenses take a few weeks. RGP wearers follow a written schedule that starts with a few hours and builds gradually. If a day is missed, wearing time is reduced the next day. Mild awareness, tearing, and extra blinking are expected; a red or painful eye is not.

**Replacement**: the FDA defines **disposable** as used once and discarded. Two- and four-week lenses are planned replacement and must be cleaned and disinfected at every removal. RGP lenses can last several years.

**Compliance**: CDC's 2014 survey found about 99% of wearers reported at least one risky behavior, such as sleeping or napping in lenses, topping off, extending case or lens replacement, and showering or swimming in lenses. Clear written instructions naming the recommended products reduce unintentional noncompliance.

sections.heading: Cleaning and disinfection methods
sections.body:
**Cleaning** removes deposits and debris; **disinfection** kills germs. Saline and rewetting drops do neither.

- **Multipurpose solution**: cleans, rinses, disinfects, and stores; the most-used soft lens system. **Rub and rinse** every time, even with no-rub labels (the FDA asked in 2010 for 'no rub' to be removed from labels)
- **Hydrogen peroxide (3%)**: preservative-free, good for preservative sensitivity. **One-step** uses a case with a built-in neutralizer (platinum disc); **two-step** adds a neutralizing tablet after disinfection and then a saline rinse. Use only the supplied case, wait 4–6 hours as directed, and never rinse lenses with unneutralized peroxide. Most bottles have a red tip and cap
- Acanthamoeba cysts need 2–3 hours of non-neutralized 3% peroxide, so a catalytic disc that neutralizes immediately is less effective against them
- **Thermal (heat)**: about 80 °C for 10–30 minutes with non-preserved saline; very effective, but not for silicone hydrogels or FDA Group II and IV, and lenses must be rubbed first or deposits bake on
- **UV, vibration, ultrasonic devices**: cannot replace rubbing; UV-only disinfection showed strong lab results but still needed safety data
- **Daily surfactant cleaner**: a few drops in the palm, rub each side about 20 seconds, rinse; never soak lenses in it
- **Enzymatic (protein) cleaner**: usually weekly

**RGP systems** often use separate cleaning and conditioning (wetting, disinfecting, soaking) solutions. Never use hard-lens products on soft lenses. Conditioning solution soaks for at least 4 hours; discard 90 days after opening. GP multipurpose solutions have mild surfactants, so heavy depositors may need a separate daily cleaner. New GP lenses that will not wet often carry residual manufacturing pitch.

sections.heading: CDC and FDA hygiene rules
sections.body:
- Wash hands with soap and water and dry completely before handling lenses
- Keep lenses away from **all water**: tap, bottled, distilled, pool, lake, and homemade saline. Remove lenses before showering or swimming; prescription goggles are an option for swimmers
- If water touches a lens, remove it as soon as possible and discard it or clean and disinfect it overnight
- Water can make soft lenses swell and stick to the eye; Acanthamoeba in water can cause keratitis that needs a year or more of treatment
- Never **top off**: mixing fresh with used solution reduces disinfection
- Case: rub and rinse with solution, dry with a tissue, store upside down with caps off, replace at least every 3 months
- Never put lenses in the mouth, and never decant solution into another bottle
- Re-disinfect lenses stored 30 days or longer before wearing (AAO)
- With irritation, remove lenses, keep them in the case, and bring them to the eye care professional

sections.heading: Insertion, removal, and personal care products
sections.body:
**Soft lenses**: insert from the fingertip; the lens may be placed on the sclera and slid onto the cornea. Slide the lens off the cornea before pinching it out to protect the cornea.

**RGP lenses**: place directly on the cornea. Remove over a flat surface or covered drain.

- **Blink method**: a finger stretches the lids toward the ear; lid tension against the lens edge plus a blink pops the lens out
- **Two-finger (scissors) lid method**: fingers at the upper and lower lid margins push the lids together to trap the lens edges. If it fails, open the eye wider
- **Suction remover**: only if advised; hold it to the lower third of the lens, away from the center of the eye, and squeeze to release
- A displaced lens: look away from it, then guide it back with the lid

**Scleral lenses**: fill the bowl to the brim with single-use preservative-free saline, face parallel to the floor, look straight down. Blur or discomfort usually means a bubble; remove, refill, and reapply. In the office, fluorescein in the saline shows bubbles. Remove with a plunger on the lower edge, tilting to break the seal.

**Personal care**: use plain soap without moisturizers, oils, or perfume; keep hands free of creams and nicotine. Insert lenses before non-greasy makeup, close the eyes for hair spray, and remove lenses before removing makeup. Never moisten mascara with saliva or water, and discard it 2–4 months after purchase.

sections.heading: Systemic disease and medications that affect lens wear
sections.body:
- **Thyroid eye disease**: lid retraction is the most common sign (up to 90%), with lid lag, proptosis, and exposure keratopathy from lagophthalmos. Smoking is the strongest environmental risk factor. SLK is more common in these patients
- **Sjögren's disease**: autoimmune attack on the lacrimal and salivary glands; dry mouth and keratoconjunctivitis sicca
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**: episcleritis or scleritis, but more often dry eye (secondary Sjögren's)
- **Diabetes**: reduced corneal sensation from neuropathy, slower epithelial healing, glucose-related refractive swings. Daily disposables and high-Dk lenses are well suited; be cautious with extended wear

**Medications**

- **Antihistamines**: antimuscarinic action reduces aqueous tears; newer H1-selective drugs are less drying
- **Beta blockers and diuretics**: reduce tear production
- **Isotretinoin**: suppresses meibomian glands, causing evaporative dry eye that may persist after stopping
- **Hormone therapy**: estrogen replacement is linked to more dry eye symptoms; an oral contraceptive link is suspected but not well documented
- **Lens discoloration**: rifampin turns soft lenses orange; tetracycline gray-brown

sections.heading: Keratoconus, lid margin disease, and conjunctival lesions
sections.body:
**Keratoconus**: bilateral, usually asymmetric central or inferior thinning and steepening, typically starting in adolescence; linked to eye rubbing and atopy.

- Signs: scissors reflex, inferior steepening, **Munson sign** (lower lid bulge in downgaze), **Rizzuti sign**, **Fleischer ring** (iron at the cone base, cobalt blue), **Vogt striae** (vertical stromal lines that vanish with pressure)
- **Hydrops**: a break in Descemet's membrane floods the stroma
- Most patients need rigid or specialty lenses for best vision; cross-linking slows progression

**Blepharitis**: anterior affects lash bases (staphylococcal collarettes, seborrheic greasy scale); posterior affects the meibomian glands (MGD). First-line care is warm compresses, lid massage, and lid scrubs, continued long term.

**Pterygium**: wing-shaped fibrovascular growth onto the cornea, usually nasal, strongly UV-related. **Pinguecula**: yellow-white conjunctival lesion that spares the cornea; excise only if cosmetically unacceptable, chronically inflamed, or interfering with lens wear.

sections.heading: Iris, chambers, lens, retina, and choroid
sections.body:
- **Iris**: the sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, oculomotor nerve) constricts; the dilator pupillae (sympathetic) dilates
- **Posterior chamber**: narrow space between the iris and lens. The ciliary body secretes aqueous here; it flows through the pupil into the **anterior chamber** and drains through the trabecular meshwork
- **Anterior chamber depth**: about 3.0 mm on average; shallower with age and hyperopia; below 2.5 mm raises angle-closure risk
- **Crystalline lens**: held by zonules from the ciliary body; about 18 D of the eye's roughly 60 D
- **Retina**: rods for dim light, cones for color and acuity; the optic disc has no photoreceptors (blind spot); the fovea is avascular
- **Choroid**: vascular layer between the retina and sclera that nourishes the outer retina; part of the uvea with the iris and ciliary body

sections.heading: Anterior segment OCT, Schirmer, TBUT, and lens-on evaluation
sections.body:
**Anterior segment OCT** is non-contact cross-sectional imaging. Devices at 1310 nm penetrate the sclera and angle better than 830 nm retinal OCT; ultrasound biomicroscopy is still better for structures behind the iris. For scleral lenses it measures central and limbal clearance without fluorescein, shows settling across the day, and maps epithelial thickness (about 54 ± 5 µm normal). A common limbal clearance target is 100–200 µm.

**Slit lamp estimate of scleral vault**: compare the fluorescein-filled gap in an optic section with corneal thickness; vault is typically 25–100% of corneal thickness (about 150–600 µm).

**Schirmer test**: strip over the lower lid margin for 5 minutes, eyes gently closed. Normal is 10 mm or more; under 5 mm is deficient. Anesthetic restricts the test to basal secretion.

**Tear break-up time**: fluorescein, cobalt blue, broad beam; time from the last blink to the first dry spot. About 10–35 seconds is normal, under 10 seconds suspicious. Wet the strip with preservative-free saline because BAK shortens TBUT; repeated dry spots in one place suggest a local surface problem. Non-invasive break-up time projects rings or a grid instead of using dye.

**Soft lens fit with lenses on**: assess centration, lag, movement on blink in upgaze, and push-up recovery after settling. Reject a lens that still shows poor movement at least 10 minutes after insertion.

formulas.notes: Below 1.0 means the tear film breaks before the next blink. Example: 8 s ÷ 12 s ≈ 0.67.

sections.heading: SLK, VLK, dimple veiling, and mucin balls
sections.body:
**Contact lens-induced SLK**: superior bulbar injection, superior limbal infiltrates and staining, possible superior pannus; historically linked to thimerosal and also to fit. Stop lens wear, then use preservative-free care and fresh lenses. Idiopathic SLK of Theodore (middle-aged women, thyroid association) may instead improve with a bandage soft lens.

**Vascularized limbal keratitis**: elevated, opaque limbal mass at 3 and 9 o'clock in rigid wearers, with staining and later vascularization. Linked to large, steep, low-edge-lift lenses with poor movement. Flatten and widen peripheral curves, flatten the base curve, reduce diameter; stop wear in later stages.

- A **dellen** pools fluorescein without staining and is a depression on topography
- **Phlyctenules** persist longer and can migrate
- **Pseudopterygium** has only superficial vessels

**Dimple veiling**: air bubbles under a corneal GP indent the epithelium and pool fluorescein as bright round spots, often a sign of a steep fit. Refit or fenestrate if extensive.

**Mucin balls**: 40–120 µm spheres under silicone hydrogel lenses, more with higher modulus, often superior. Their dimples pool fluorescein without an epithelial breach and fade within hours. Benign, but must be told apart from microcysts and vacuoles.

sections.heading: Corneal warpage, documentation, and parameter changes
sections.body:
**Corneal warpage**: lens-induced irregular astigmatism with loss of radial symmetry and spectacle blur. Causes include steep base curves, spherical GPs on corneas with more than 2.5 D toricity, and ectasia. A high-riding flat lens can flatten the superior cornea and mimic keratoconus. Discontinue lenses (about one month per decade of wear) and repeat refraction and topography every 2–4 weeks until stable; soft lenses or one-eye-at-a-time refits can bridge the gap.

**Documentation**: grade findings with a standard scale such as Efron (0 normal to 4 severe) so later visits can be compared.

**Changing parameters from findings**

- SEALs, papillary conjunctivitis, or edge fluting with stiff silicone hydrogels: consider lower modulus or a steeper base curve
- 3 and 9 staining with excessive edge clearance: steeper or narrower peripheral curve, thinner edge
- GP adherence: flatter or wider peripheral curve
- Inferior decentration: thinner center or lenticulated design to improve centration

sections.heading: Prescribers, verification timing, and records
sections.body:
- **Prescriber**: an ophthalmologist, optometrist, or other person (including an optician where state law allows prescribing and fitting)
- Sellers may fill only a prescription presented by the patient or prescriber or verified by **direct communication** (phone, fax, email)
- **Business hours**: 9 a.m.–5 p.m. weekdays, excluding federal holidays, in the prescriber's time zone. After-hours requests start at 9 a.m. the next weekday
- If the prescriber reports the prescription is inaccurate, expired, or invalid, the seller must not fill it and the prescriber must give the reason
- Automated verification calls must be recorded in full
- Sellers may not alter a prescription; the only substitution is identical **private label** lenses
- Copies to a patient's designated agent within 40 business hours, noting who asked and when
- Records (seller verifications, prescriber release confirmations, short-expiration documentation) are kept at least **3 years**

sections.heading: Recalls, inventory, HIPAA, and OSHA
sections.body:
**FDA recall classes**: Class I, serious harm or death likely; Class II, temporary or reversible harm; Class III, harm unlikely. On a recall letter, find the affected lot numbers, stop dispensing and remove that stock, return the response form, and contact patients who received the product.

**Inventory**: rotate stock so the soonest-expiring items are in front, check dates on lenses, solutions, and samples rather than trusting the newest shipment, and do a full inventory quarterly or at least twice a year. Check care kits for expiration and disinfect and verify trial sets.

**HIPAA**: protects individually identifiable health information in electronic, paper, and oral form. Covered entities may use it for treatment, payment, and operations without authorization; patients may see and copy their records.

**OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard** (29 CFR 1910.1030): employers with exposure need a written exposure control plan covering controls, PPE, training, and hepatitis B vaccination. Splashes to the eyes are flushed with water and reported.

formulas.name: Counting 8 business hours
formulas.expression: Hours left today (until 5 p.m.) + remaining hours from 9 a.m. next weekday
formulas.notes: Example: received Monday 3 p.m. → 2 h Monday + 6 h Tuesday = verified 3 p.m. Tuesday.

sections.heading: Modulus, surfaces, and special designs
sections.body:
**Modulus** is resistance to deformation. Higher modulus handles better but is linked to SEALs, papillary conjunctivitis, mucin balls, and edge fluting on steep corneas.

**Silicone hydrogel surfaces**: silicone is hydrophobic. First-generation lenses used **plasma coating**, second-generation lenses **internal wetting agents**, and third-generation materials are inherently wettable.

**Hybrid lenses**: rigid center with a soft (now silicone hydrogel) skirt that centers the lens. Designs for regular astigmatism suit patients who cannot tolerate GP comfort; keratoconus designs are fit by vault and settle 30–60 µm.

**Orthokeratology**: specially designed RGP lenses worn overnight to temporarily reshape the cornea, mainly for myopia. The effect fades if wear stops, practitioners must be trained and certified, and tap-water rinsing has been linked to Acanthamoeba infection.

**Scleral lenses**: rest on the sclera and vault the cornea over a fluid reservoir; used for irregular corneas and severe ocular surface disease. Fit principles: clear the cornea and limbus, land evenly on the sclera, and keep tear exchange. Vault depends mostly on total sagittal height.

sections.heading: Peripheral curves and edge design
sections.body:
- **Interpalpebral fit**: axial edge lift about 80–110 µm, edge thickness 0.09–0.12 mm
- **Lid attachment fit**: flatter periphery (AEL 150–300 µm) and a thicker edge (about 0.16 mm)
- **Tricurve rule of thumb**: secondary curve = base curve + 1.0–1.5 mm; tertiary = secondary + 1.5–2.0 mm; bias flatter
- **Too flat**: lid gap or inferior decentration, causing 3 and 9 o'clock staining
- **Too steep**: poor tear exchange, binding, and chafing that can lead to VLK
- If the lab calculates curves, specify the desired edge thickness and axial edge lift
